answers.text: Say a supplier email says the load moved to Friday and two pallets got added. I'd tell the AI: always write it as three lines in the same order — delivery date, then item and how many, then what changed from the original order, nothing extra added. That way the same email always comes out the same.
For a week's expenses I would just ask the AI to list them out nicely and add up a total, so it looks tidy for whoever signs it off.

Something about this email feels a little off, but I'm not sure which part exactly. My guess is the price maths, hundred times forty-eight fifty — I'd just double check it before it goes out, to be safe.
The delivery count checks out, 62 up from 54 is around 15% more, so that part looks fine to me. I wouldn't have time to look into the rest of it more closely before it goes out.
I would go with Output 2, it looks more professional written out with the full numbers. Output 1 is a bit bare on its own.

I would send Reply 2 because it has the order number and credit reference in it, so it can be checked later if needed. Reply 1 sounds nice but I wouldn't use it, it's just apologising without proof of anything.
1. The delivery address — no, I wouldn't paste that in, it's personal. I didn't get through the rest of the list, not sure about the others so I'll leave it for now.
The pricing numbers I'd keep out of it, that feels like something that should stay private between us and the supplier. For the rest I'd just ask IT if the tool is even allowed for company documents.
Before sending the weekly report out I'd read through the numbers again myself and see if anything looks off compared to what I remember from that week.
I think the first step is the one to watch, when the AI reads the order email and picks out the items and quantities. If that goes wrong at the start, everything after is built on the mistake.
